name: Large-scale data art / environmental AI models
originator: Primary practitioners: Refik Anadol (Large Nature Model, Dataland museum, RAS Studio), Holly Herndon & Mat Dryhurst (Holly+ voice model, Spawning AI), Jake Elwes (Zizi Project, queer AI datasets), Sofia Crespo (neural network art trained on biological datasets), Anna Ridler (Mosaic Virus, hand-built datasets). Emerging category includes artists building custom AI models trained on domain-specific environmental, ecological, or cultural datasets.
geography: Global. Anadol based in Los Angeles (Dataland museum opening 2026). Herndon & Dryhurst in Berlin. Crespo in various locations. The practice spans major art institutions worldwide: Guggenheim, MoMA, V&A, Serpentine, NGV. UN partnerships (Anadol's Large Nature Model presented at UNEP). Institutional presence concentrated in US, Europe, and major international biennials.
core_claim: Artists can and should build their own AI models trained on domain-specific datasets rather than relying on corporate foundation models. The artist-as-model-builder creates AI infrastructure that serves artistic, ecological, and public purposes. Anadol's Large Nature Model -- trained on millions of nature images and released as open source -- proposes that artist-built AI can become public resource, not just artistic output. The practice argues that the dataset is the artwork's foundation, and curating datasets is a creative act with ethical and political dimensions.
medium_specificity: Fully digitally native in computation, hybrid in output. The core creative act -- training an AI model on a curated dataset -- is entirely digital and could not exist outside computational infrastructure. The outputs range from immersive installations (Anadol's large-scale projections) to screen-based works (Crespo's neural network organisms) to voice models (Holly+) to physical artifacts. What makes this practice digitally specific is not the output format but the creative process: dataset curation + model architecture + training = the artwork's generative core. The model itself is the medium.
relation_to_attention_economy: Complex and stratified. Anadol's immersive installations are attention-economy powerhouses (MoMA's Unsupervised attracted nearly 3 million visitors). The spectacle of large-scale data visualization generates enormous media attention. However, the underlying practice -- building custom models, curating datasets, releasing open-source infrastructure -- serves structural needs that operate beneath the attention surface. Herndon & Dryhurst's Spawning AI (Have I Been Trained) is explicitly anti-attention-economy: it provides consent infrastructure. Ridler's hand-built datasets resist algorithmic scale. The practice spans from maximum spectacle (Anadol) to maximum infrastructure (Spawning).
relation_to_intention: Strongly intention-native at the infrastructure level. Building a domain-specific AI model serves declared structural needs: representing underrepresented data (ecological, cultural, biological), creating alternatives to corporate AI monoculture, and providing public AI infrastructure. Anadol's open-sourcing of the Large Nature Model and UN partnership signal intention to serve public good. Herndon's consent tools serve declared field needs. However, the exhibition and spectacle layer of the practice (Anadol's museum, immersive installations) serves attention dynamics. The practice operates on two levels: intention-native infrastructure underneath attention-capturing spectacle.
revenue_model: Multiple streams. Anadol: NFT sales (significant -- Unsupervised series, Living Architecture), museum commissions, Dataland museum revenue (tickets, partnerships), corporate commissions, speaking fees. Herndon: Spawning AI venture funding, Holly+ NFT sales, performance fees. Crespo: gallery sales, NFT sales, commissions. Ridler: gallery sales, commissions, grants. The revenue model varies dramatically across practitioners -- from Anadol's institutional-scale operation to Ridler's grant-supported practice. The open-source model release (Large Nature Model) is not directly monetized but builds cultural capital and institutional partnerships. [uncertain]
market_position: Institutional exhibition and primary market. Museum commissions and acquisitions (MoMA, Guggenheim, V&A, Serpentine). Gallery sales for physical and digital works. NFT market for digital editions. The practice operates at the intersection of institutional art, technology industry, and emerging AI art market. Anadol occupies the premium tier; other practitioners range across the market.
price_range: Wide range. Anadol's NFT works: significant sums (Unsupervised at MoMA level). Physical installations: museum commission scale ($100K-$1M+). Other practitioners: gallery-level prices ($1K-$50K for works). The market values both the spectacle output and the conceptual framework of artist-built AI. Premium pricing for practitioners with institutional validation. [uncertain]
volume_trend_2024_2026: Growing strongly. AI art is the most culturally visible art category in 2024-2026. Anadol's Dataland museum (opening Spring 2026) represents institutional scaling. The Large Nature Model's UN presentation and open-source release signal growing public infrastructure ambitions. Institutional acquisitions increasing. The practice benefits from AI as a dominant cultural discourse. Risk: the category could be diluted by the flood of AI-generated art using corporate models -- the distinction between 'artist builds model' and 'artist uses model' matters but is not widely understood. [uncertain]
collector_demographics: Institutional buyers (museums, foundations). High-net-worth collectors interested in technology and contemporary art. Crypto-native collectors for NFT works. Corporate collections. A growing audience of AI-literate collectors who understand the distinction between custom model-building and prompt engineering. The Dataland museum targets a broader public audience (3M visitors expected based on MoMA precedent). [uncertain]
sustainability: Strong for established practitioners, uncertain for the category. Anadol has achieved institutional sustainability (museum, major partnerships, Google/UN backing). Herndon has Spawning AI as a venture-funded enterprise. Other practitioners depend on grants, gallery sales, and commissions -- standard art market sustainability. The category's sustainability depends on whether 'artist-built AI models' remains a distinct and valued practice as corporate AI tools become ubiquitous. The open-source model contribution (Large Nature Model) may create long-term cultural capital even if not directly monetized.
toolchain: Custom AI/ML pipelines. Python-based machine learning frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow). Custom dataset curation tools and processes. High-performance computing for model training (GPU clusters). Anadol: custom studio pipeline, Google partnerships for compute. Herndon: custom voice synthesis models. Crespo: GAN and diffusion model architectures. Ridler: hand-curated datasets with standard ML tools. Output rendering: Unity, TouchDesigner, custom visualization software, large-scale projection and LED hardware for immersive installations. The toolchain requires significant technical expertise and computational resources.
relation_to_AI: AI is the primary medium -- but the relationship is as builder, not user. These artists do not use DALL-E, Midjourney, or Stable Diffusion as creative tools. They build their own models with intentional datasets. This distinction is fundamental: the artist controls the training data, model architecture, and generative process at a structural level. The practice implicitly critiques corporate AI by demonstrating alternative models built on different values (ecological data, consent-based data, culturally specific data). The Large Nature Model is both artwork and AI infrastructure. Holly+ is both voice art and consent tool.
liveness: Mixed. Immersive installations: real-time generative (Anadol's data sculptures evolve continuously). Holly+: live performance and ongoing voice synthesis. Neural network outputs: typically generated and then static. Model training: a temporal process with its own duration and rhythm. The models themselves are 'live' in that they can continuously generate new outputs. Exhibition installations combine generative liveness with spectacle scale.
aesthetic_vocabulary: Forming and significant. Key terms: 'data painting,' 'data sculpture,' 'machine hallucination,' 'latent space,' 'dataset as artwork,' 'model as medium,' 'artist-as-model-builder,' 'consent-based AI,' 'open-source AI art.' Anadol has contributed 'machine dreams' and 'machine hallucinations' to popular vocabulary. Herndon has contributed 'consent layer' and 'data dignity.' Ridler's concept of hand-curated datasets as artistic practice is influential. The vocabulary bridges AI research, art criticism, environmental science, and ethics. It is still forming -- the distinction between 'using AI' and 'building AI' lacks established critical language.
tendency_axis_position: Openness <-> Enclosure: Split. Large Nature Model is open-source (radical openness). Anadol Studio's proprietary pipeline is enclosed. Spawning AI provides open consent tools. The practice contains both tendencies. | Commons <-> Capture: Strong commons contribution at infrastructure level (open models, consent tools). Capture at exhibition level (premium pricing, institutional exclusivity). | Spectacle <-> Infrastructure: Both simultaneously. Anadol's installations are maximum spectacle; the underlying open-source model and UN partnership are maximum infrastructure. | Individual <-> Collective: Individual artist practice (Anadol as brand) but the open-source model and consent tools serve collective needs. The practice's most significant contributions are collective infrastructure disguised as individual art.
openness: Significantly open at the infrastructure level. Large Nature Model: open-source release for public use. Spawning AI: open consent tools (Have I Been Trained). Herndon's Holly+ model has open components. However, individual studio practices are often proprietary (Anadol Studio's pipeline, Crespo's specific techniques). The practice's most important contribution -- open AI models as public resource -- is genuinely open. The exhibition and commercial layer is standard art market enclosure.
governance_model: Individual artist/studio practice. No shared governance across the movement. Each artist governs their own practice, datasets, and model releases. Anadol: studio with team, increasingly institutional (Dataland board and partners). Herndon: Spawning AI has startup governance. Open-source model releases create de facto commons governance (anyone can use, modify, fork). The Large Nature Model's open-source release creates a public governance question: who maintains and develops the model going forward?
data_sovereignty: Central concern. Dataset curation is the core creative act, and questions of data sovereignty -- who owns the training data, who consented to its use, who benefits from the model -- are explicit themes. Herndon's Spawning AI (Have I Been Trained) is directly about data sovereignty for artists whose work is used in AI training. Anadol's nature datasets raise questions about ecological data sovereignty. Ridler's hand-built datasets demonstrate maximum artist sovereignty over training data. The practice is the most data-sovereignty-conscious in the AI art field.
interoperability: Moderate. Open-source models (Large Nature Model) are interoperable by design -- anyone can download, use, and build on them. Standard ML frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow) ensure technical interoperability. However, immersive installations are site-specific and not portable. Each artist's pipeline is custom and not interoperable with others. The open-source model releases are the most interoperable contribution.
preservation_strategy: Mixed. Physical installations: temporary by nature (site-specific, technology-dependent). Digital works and NFTs: standard blockchain preservation for tokens, IPFS for media. AI models: open-source releases on GitHub/Hugging Face provide preservation through distribution. The Large Nature Model's open-source status means it is preserved across many copies. Training datasets may face preservation challenges (storage costs, rights management). Museum acquisitions (MoMA, Guggenheim) provide institutional preservation for specific works. The broader practice faces the challenge of preserving complex computational systems -- a model is not just code but training data, hyperparameters, and computational environment.
consent_architecture: The most advanced consent thinking in the AI art field. Herndon & Dryhurst's Spawning AI / Have I Been Trained provides explicit consent infrastructure for artists regarding AI training data. The concept of consent-based AI (artists choose whether their work trains AI models) originated from this practice. Anadol's use of nature data sidesteps human consent questions but raises ecological data ethics. Ridler's hand-built datasets represent maximum consent control (the artist curated every image). The practice has contributed more to consent architecture discourse than any other AI art category.
relation_to_traditional_art_world: Deeply integrated at the institutional level. MoMA acquisition of Anadol's Unsupervised. Guggenheim exhibitions. V&A collection. Serpentine programming. Venice Biennale presence. Major gallery representation. The practice has achieved the highest level of traditional art world integration among AI art forms, partly because of its scale and spectacle, partly because the conceptual depth (dataset-as-medium, model-as-artwork) resonates with contemporary art discourse. Anadol's Dataland museum represents the ultimate integration: an artist-founded museum in LA's museum district.
what_it_enables: A new category: artist-as-model-builder. Demonstrates that artists can create AI infrastructure, not just AI outputs. Open-source model releases create public AI resources that serve non-commercial purposes (environmental monitoring, conservation, education). Consent infrastructure (Spawning AI) for the entire field. Proves that domain-specific AI models (trained on nature, ecology, specific cultures) can produce results that corporate general-purpose models cannot. Creates a model for how AI can serve artistic and public purposes rather than only commercial ones.
what_it_lacks: Accessibility -- building custom AI models requires significant technical expertise and computational resources. Critical engagement with the environmental cost of model training (GPU compute is energy-intensive). Shared infrastructure or standards across practitioners (each artist builds from scratch). Community beyond individual studio practices. Engagement with the distinction between spectacle and infrastructure in public discourse (Anadol's spectacle gets attention; the open-source model gets less). The category lacks a critical framework that distinguishes 'artist builds meaningful model' from 'artist trains model as marketing claim.'
who_is_excluded: Artists without AI/ML expertise or engineering collaborators. Artists without access to GPU compute (expensive). Artists without institutional support for large-scale practice. Communities without academic or tech industry connections. The environmental cost of model training creates a sustainability contradiction (training models to represent nature consumes energy). Small-scale practitioners are excluded from the spectacle-scale presentation that generates institutional attention. Artists in the Global South face particular barriers (compute access, institutional networks, dataset availability). [uncertain]
frontier_signal: Frontier, establishing a new category. The concept of 'artist-as-model-builder' is genuinely new and challenges existing categories. The Large Nature Model's open-source release and UN partnership establish a precedent for artist-built AI as public infrastructure. Dataland museum (2026) represents institutional scaling of the category. The question being tested: can artist-built AI models become as culturally significant as the artworks they produce? If yes, this creates an entirely new art practice category where the model is the artwork and the outputs are demonstrations.
discovery_mechanism: Museum exhibitions (primary for established practitioners), mainstream media coverage (AI art generates significant press), institutional partnerships (UN, Google, Serpentine), social media (immersive installations perform well online), academic publications and conferences, art world networks. The spectacle dimension ensures broad discovery. The infrastructure dimension (open-source models, consent tools) is discovered through tech and research channels.
attention_dependency: Stratified. Immersive installations: high attention dependency (require visitor footfall and media coverage). Open-source model releases: low attention dependency (utility-driven adoption). Consent tools (Spawning AI): low attention dependency (solve a real problem). The practice's cultural impact depends on the spectacle layer's attention capture, but the structural contributions (open models, consent tools) survive independently of attention cycles.
intention_alignment: Strongly intention-native at the infrastructure level. Building open-source AI models for environmental and cultural purposes serves declared structural needs. Consent tools serve declared field needs. The practice explicitly intends to create alternatives to corporate AI monoculture. At the exhibition level, the practice serves institutional attention needs. The most important contributions (open models, consent architecture, dataset ethics) are intention-native.
commons_contribution: The highest commons contribution in the AI art field. Large Nature Model: open-source AI infrastructure for anyone. Spawning AI: open consent tools for the entire creative field. Dataset ethics discourse: public knowledge contribution. The practice's signature contribution is turning artist practice into public infrastructure -- models, tools, and frameworks that serve beyond the artist's own work. This is genuinely novel and significant.
provenance_type: Both ownership and meaning, with unique dataset provenance. The training dataset itself becomes a provenance layer -- where the data came from, who curated it, what it represents. This is a new form of provenance: provenance of training data as artistic and ethical documentation. Ownership provenance via standard art market and blockchain channels. Meaning provenance through institutional exhibition history and critical reception. The dataset provenance dimension is the most significant contribution to provenance discourse.
temporal_logic: Deep-historical and anticipatory. Datasets encode historical information (millions of nature images spanning decades). The models project forward -- generative capacity implies future outputs. Training is a temporal process (days/weeks of computation). Open-source releases create an ongoing temporal dimension (the model continues to be used and adapted after release). Anadol's 'machine dreams' concept implies a temporal logic of processing and transformation that operates on its own timeline.
absence_handling: Partially addresses absence. Environmental AI models represent ecological data that is typically absent from art discourse. Domain-specific datasets surface underrepresented information. Consent tools make visible the absence of consent in corporate AI training. However, the practice does not systematically address its own absences: whose environments are not represented in the data? Whose ecological knowledge is excluded? The Large Nature Model's dataset curation inevitably excludes some ecosystems and perspectives.
coherence_vs_consensus: Coherence. The practitioners share a coherent set of concerns (dataset ethics, model-as-medium, artist sovereignty over AI) while pursuing diverse approaches. No consensus-seeking mechanism. Multiple valid positions coexist: Anadol's spectacle-infrastructure hybrid, Herndon's consent-first approach, Ridler's small-scale dataset curation, Crespo's biological aesthetics. Coherent in questions, diverse in answers.
contestability: High. The central claims are actively contested: Is training an AI model really artistic practice? Is Anadol's spectacle substantive or decorative? Is open-sourcing a model enough to qualify as public infrastructure? The AI art community, traditional art critics, and AI researchers all contest different aspects. This contestability is productive -- it refines the practice and its claims. Open-source model releases are themselves contestable (anyone can examine, critique, or improve the model).
forkability: High for open-source contributions. The Large Nature Model can be forked, retrained, or adapted by anyone. Spawning AI tools can be replicated. The conceptual framework (artist builds domain-specific model) is infinitely forkable. However, the spectacle dimension (immersive installations, museum presence) requires institutional relationships and resources that cannot be forked. The open-source contributions are the most forkable element of any practice in this research.
what_adai_should_adopt: The concept of artist-built AI as public infrastructure is directly relevant to A(DAI)'s mission. The Large Nature Model demonstrates that AI models can serve artistic, ecological, and public purposes simultaneously -- A(DAI) should study this for its own intelligence infrastructure. Herndon's consent architecture (Spawning AI, Have I Been Trained) provides a model for A(DAI)'s consent layer. The dataset-as-creative-act concept aligns with A(DAI)'s emphasis on curating field intelligence. The open-source model release model shows how artistic practice can contribute to commons without sacrificing artistic identity. The provenance-of-training-data concept extends A(DAI)'s provenance-of-meaning framework into AI-specific territory.
what_adai_should_refuse: The individual-artist-as-brand model (Anadol as celebrity) that concentrates cultural authority. The spectacle-first presentation that risks reducing structural contributions to entertainment. The resource-intensive approach that excludes most practitioners. The uncritical celebration of AI capabilities without examining environmental costs, data biases, and power dynamics. The implicit hierarchy where spectacle-scale practice receives institutional attention while small-scale, critical work is marginalized. The corporate partnership dependencies (Google compute, UN institutional framing) that may compromise independence.
structural_tension: This practice proves that artist-built AI models can become public infrastructure -- but the artists who achieve this operate at institutional scale with corporate backing, creating exactly the kind of centralized authority that commons-first approaches should resist. A(DAI) faces the same tension: building meaningful AI infrastructure requires computational resources and institutional partnerships that may compromise independence. The deeper tension: can collective intelligence infrastructure be built from below (many contributors, small datasets, distributed compute) or does meaningful AI require the scale that only corporate or institutional partnerships provide? The Large Nature Model is individual genius creating commons; A(DAI) wants collective process creating commons. Whether the collective approach can match the individual's impact is the open question.
regulatory_exposure: Moderate and increasing. EU AI Act applies to AI models depending on classification (the Large Nature Model could be considered a general-purpose AI model requiring transparency). Copyright questions around training data are central to the practice (Herndon's Spawning AI directly addresses this). DMCA and copyright opt-out regimes are highly relevant. The practice is more exposed to AI-specific regulation than other art forms because it involves actual model building, not just AI-tool use. Environmental data used in models may face data protection or sovereignty regulations depending on jurisdiction. The open-source release model has regulatory implications (model distribution, liability for downstream use). [uncertain]
ip_model: Complex and varied. Anadol: retains copyright on outputs, open-source license for Large Nature Model. Herndon: open tools (Spawning AI), copyright on artistic works. Training data IP: the central unresolved question -- using copyrighted images to train models is legally contested globally. Open-source model releases use standard software licenses (MIT, Apache). The practice is at the forefront of AI IP debates and is actively shaping legal and cultural norms around AI training data rights.
opt_in_vs_opt_out: The practice is defining the opt-in/opt-out debate for AI. Herndon's Spawning AI provides opt-out tools for artists (Have I Been Trained). The concept of consent-based AI training data originates from this practice. Anadol's use of nature images raises different consent questions (nature cannot opt in or out). The practice spans the full spectrum: from maximum consent (Ridler's hand-curated datasets) to contested consent (large-scale scraping) to non-applicable consent (environmental data). This is the art field's most significant contribution to the opt-in/opt-out regulatory conversation.
platform_dependency: Depends on GPU compute infrastructure (cloud providers: Google Cloud, AWS, or local clusters). GitHub/Hugging Face for model distribution. Exhibition venues for spectacle output. Standard web infrastructure. No blockchain dependency for most practitioners (some NFT sales). The compute dependency is the most significant -- model training requires access to expensive, energy-intensive infrastructure. Google partnership (Anadol) reduces cost but creates dependency. Smaller practitioners face compute access as a primary barrier.
network_effects: Moderate and growing. Open-source model releases create network effects (more users improve and extend the model). Spawning AI creates consent-network effects (more artists registering creates more comprehensive consent data). Institutional exhibitions create cultural network effects (museum shows validate the practice, attracting more institutional interest). However, the practice is not a platform -- network effects operate through shared concepts and open infrastructure rather than marketplace dynamics.
post_crash_trajectory: Growing strongly, largely independent of NFT crash. The practice's value proposition (artist-built AI as public infrastructure) became more relevant post-crash as the field moved from speculation to substance. Institutional interest accelerated: MoMA acquisition, Guggenheim exhibitions, Dataland museum, UN partnership. Anadol's trajectory is sharply upward. Herndon's Spawning AI gained cultural significance as AI consent debates intensified. The practice benefits from AI as the dominant cultural discourse of 2024-2026. NFT-specific sales may have declined but institutional and traditional market value increased.
